for: Everyone who has broken something or knows who did (the fracture hit's pull: 'which one have you had?'). They send it to the friend who punched a wall: the first type is that exact break.
title: 6 fractures and how you get them
question: 6 fractures and how people get them. Which one have you had?
hook: Punch a wall, and *this* is the bone that usually breaks.

why: Boxer's fracture: punching something hard with a closed fist breaks the neck of the hand bone behind the pinky knuckle (5th metacarpal); the knuckle can look sunken. Colles' fracture: a fall on an outstretched hand breaks the end of the radius at the wrist and the broken end tilts toward the back of the hand. Smith's fracture: the reverse, often from a fall on a bent wrist; the broken end tilts toward the palm. Scaphoid fracture: a fall on an outstretched hand breaks a small wrist bone; it can be invisible on the first X-ray, so pain at the base of the thumb (the snuffbox) gets a splint and a second X-ray. Nightstick fracture: a blow to a raised forearm breaks the ulna on its own (named for blocking a police baton). March fracture: a stress fracture of a foot bone (usually the 2nd or 3rd metatarsal) from repeated pounding, first described in 1855 in Prussian soldiers on long marches. Pain that won't quit after a hit or a fall: get it checked.
